questions.question: RAPTOR embeds the text chunks that become the leaf nodes of its tree with one specific off-the-shelf sentence encoder. In the paper that introduced that encoder, how long does clustering 10,000 sentences with hierarchical clustering take with the original BERT, and what does the newly introduced model reduce that effort to?
questions.expected_answer: RAPTOR's leaf chunks are embedded with SBERT (multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1, Reimers & Gurevych 2019). The Sentence-BERT paper states that clustering 10,000 sentences with hierarchical clustering requires about 65 hours with BERT, because around 50 million sentence combinations must be computed, and that with SBERT the effort was reduced to about 5 seconds.
questions.rationale: Paper A (raptor) is the only place that says which encoder produces the leaf-node embeddings (SBERT); paper B (sbert) is the only place that quantifies the 65 hours -> 5 seconds speed-up. The bridging entity SBERT is never named in the question.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: RAPTOR embeds its text chunks with SBERT, a BERT-based encoder (multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1, Reimers & Gurevych 2019), and those chunks plus their SBERT embeddings form the leaf nodes of its tree.

spans.quote:
These texts
are then embedded using SBERT, a BERT-based encoder ( multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1)
(Reimers & Gurevych, 2019). The chunks and their corresponding SBERT embeddings form the
leaf nodes of our tree structure.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The Sentence-BERT paper reports that clustering 10,000 sentences with hierarchical clustering takes about 65 hours with BERT (around 50 million sentence combinations) and that SBERT reduces the effort to about 5 seconds.

spans.quote:
For exam-
ple, clustering of 10,000 sentences with hierarchi-
cal clustering requires with BERT about 65 hours,
as around 50 Million sentence combinations must
be computed. With SBERT, we were able to re-

questions.question: REPLUG plugs in an existing dense retrieval model as its retriever and initializes REPLUG LSR from that same model. According to that retriever's own paper, how are the positive pairs of its unsupervised contrastive training built, and where do its negatives come from?
questions.expected_answer: REPLUG uses Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022a) and initializes REPLUG LSR with it. The Contriever paper says the model uses MoCo with random cropping: positive pairs are sampled by random cropping, with tokens of each element of the pair deleted with probability 10%, and the negatives consist of elements from previous batches stored in a queue, which allows scaling to a large number of negatives; training data comes from Wikipedia and CCNet.
questions.rationale: Paper A (replug) identifies the retriever that REPLUG uses; the construction of its positives and negatives only exists in paper B (contriever). Neither Contriever nor MoCo is named in the question.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: REPLUG uses the Contriever model as its retrieval model and initializes the REPLUG LSR retriever with the Contriever model.

spans.quote:
Following prior
work (Izacard et al., 2022b), we use the Contriever (Izacard
et al., 2022a) as the retrieval model for REPLUG, as it has
demonstrated strong performance.

For REPLUG LSR , we initialize the retriever with the
Contriever model (Izacard et al., 2022a).

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The Contriever paper states that Contriever uses MoCo with random cropping: positive pairs are sampled using random cropping with 10% token deletion, negatives are elements from previous batches stored in a queue, and training data comes from Wikipedia and CCNet.

spans.quote:
we empirically evaluate our best retriever trained with contrastive learning, calledContriever
(contrastive retriever), which uses MoCo with random cropping. We use a contrastive learning procedure that
diﬀers from ICT (Lee et al., 2019) mainly in three aspects. First, positive pairs are sampled using random
cropping and tokens from each element of the pair are deleted with a probability of 10%.

Second we use
MoCo where negatives consists of elements from previous batches stored in a queue. This allows to scale to a
large number of negatives.

questions.question: The multilingual E5 technical report says its training procedure adheres to the recipe of an earlier English embedding-model family instead of restating that recipe. In the paper that describes that earlier recipe, what filtering technique is applied to the mined text-pair corpus, and how many pairs survive it for contrastive pre-training?
questions.expected_answer: Multilingual E5 follows the English E5 recipe (Wang et al., 2022). The E5 paper applies a consistency-based filter: a model is first trained on the 1.3B noisy text pairs and then used to rank each pair against a pool of 1 million random passages, keeping a pair only if it falls in the top-k ranked lists (k = 2); after this step about 270M text pairs remain for contrastive pre-training.
questions.rationale: Paper A (multilingual-e5) points to the English E5 recipe without describing it; the consistency-based filter and the 1.3B -> ~270M reduction are only in paper B (e5). The question names neither E5 nor CCPairs.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The multilingual E5 report states that its training procedure adheres to the English E5 model recipe: contrastive pre-training on 1 billion multilingual text pairs followed by fine-tuning on a combination of labeled datasets.

spans.quote:
The
training procedure adheres to the English E5
model recipe, involving contrastive pre-training
on 1 billion multilingual text pairs, followed
by fine-tuning on a combination of labeled
datasets.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The E5 paper proposes a consistency-based data filter: a model trained on the 1.3B noisy pairs ranks each pair against 1 million random passages and keeps it only if it is in the top-k (k = 2) list, leaving about 270M text pairs for contrastive pre-training.

spans.quote:
Consistency-based filter To further improve data quality and make training costs manageable, we
propose a consistency-based data filtering technique: a model is first trained on the 1.3B noisy text
pairs, and then used to rank each pair against a pool of 1 million random passages. A text pair is kept
only if it falls in the top-k ranked lists.

Here we set k = 2 based on manual inspection of data quality. After this
step, we end up with∼ 270M text pairs for contrastive pre-training.

questions.question: With GPT3, IRCoT's interleaved retrieval improves its recall metric over one-step retrieval by 22.6 points, the largest gain among the four multi-step QA datasets it evaluates on. questions.rationale: Paper A (ircot) gives the per-dataset gains in order, which is what identifies the 22.6-point dataset as 2WikiMultihopQA; paper B (2wikimultihop) is the only source for the evidence-triple annotation and the four question types. The question names neither.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: IRCoT reports recall gains over one-step retrieval on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and IIRC of 7.9, 14.3, 3.5 and 10.2 points with Flan-T5-XXL and of 11.3, 22.6, 12.5 and 21.2 points respectively with GPT3, so the 22.6-point gain corresponds to 2WikiMultihopQA.

proves our recall metric relative to one-step re-
trieval, on HotpotQA by 7.9, on 2WikiMultihopQA

questions.question: LightRAG compares against a graph-enhanced RAG baseline that aggregates nodes into communities and produces a community report to capture global information. In that baseline's own paper, which community-detection algorithm builds those communities, and how is the hierarchy obtained?
questions.expected_answer: The baseline is GraphRAG. Its paper says the pipeline uses Leiden community detection (Traag et al., 2019) in a hierarchical manner, recursively detecting sub-communities inside each detected community until reaching leaf communities that can no longer be partitioned.
questions.rationale: Paper A (lightrag) describes the baseline by its behaviour (communities plus community reports) and that is what identifies GraphRAG; the Leiden algorithm and the recursive hierarchy are only stated in paper B (graphrag). Neither Leiden nor GraphRAG is named in the question.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: LightRAG's baseline GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) is described as a graph-enhanced RAG system that uses an LLM to extract entities and relationships as nodes and edges, aggregates nodes into communities and produces a community report to capture global information.

spans.quote:
• GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024): This is a graph-enhanced RAG system that utilizes an LLM to
extract entities and relationships from the text, representing them as nodes and edges. It generates
corresponding descriptions for these elements, aggregates nodes into communities, and produces a
community report to capture global information.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The pipeline in the paper pinned as graphrag uses Leiden community detection (Traag et al., 2019) hierarchically, recursively detecting sub-communities within each detected community until reaching leaf communities that can no longer be partitioned.

In our pipeline, we use Leiden community
detection (Traag et al., 2019) in a hierarchical manner, recursively detecting sub-communities within

we introduce MultiHop-RAG. To our knowledge,

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: MultiHop-RAG's embedding-model comparison tests ada-embeddings, voyage-02, llm-embedder, bge-large-en-v1.5, jina-embeddings-v2-base-en, e5-base-v2 and instructor-large (Su et al., 2023).

spans.quote:
In this experiment, we test a variety set of em-
bedding models, including the ada-embeddings by
OpenAI (text-embedding-ada-002, text-search-ada-
query-001), voyage-02 3, llm-embedder (Zhang
et al., 2023), bge-large-en-v1.5 (Xiao et al., 2023),
jina-embeddings-v2-base-en (Günther et al., 2023),
e5-base-v2 (Wang et al., 2022), and instructor-large
(Su et al., 2023).

questions.question: ModernBERT trains its multi-vector retrieval models with a setup it describes as an update on an earlier retriever's training procedure (Santhanam et al., 2022). questions.expected_answer: The earlier retriever is ColBERTv2. Its paper says it uses an aggressive residual compression mechanism that reduces the space footprint of late interaction by 6-10x while preserving quality, giving a footprint competitive with typical single-vector models.
questions.rationale: Paper A (modernbert) is where the cited training procedure is tied to ColBERTv2; the residual-compression mechanism and the 6-10x figure are only in paper B (colbert2). The question does not name ColBERTv2.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: ModernBERT adopts the training setup of JaColBERTv2.5, an update on the ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022) training procedure, with batch size 16 and 5% learning-rate warmup.

ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022) training
procedure, with a batch size of 16 and a 5%
learning rate warmup.

questions.question: ModernBERT trains its multi-vector retrievers by distilling the scores of a teacher embedding model cited to Chen et al. (2024). In that teacher model's own paper, which retrieval functionalities are assigned to which parts of its output, and what training framework lets them reinforce one another?
questions.expected_answer: The teacher is BGE-M3 / M3-Embedding. Its paper proposes a self-knowledge distillation framework in which the multiple retrieval functionalities are jointly learned and mutually reinforced: the [CLS] embedding is used for dense retrieval while embeddings from the other tokens are used for sparse retrieval and multi-vector retrieval, and the relevance scores from the different retrieval functions are integrated into a teacher signal used for knowledge distillation.
questions.rationale: Paper A (modernbert) is where the teacher model used for distillation is identified; its three retrieval functionalities and the self-knowledge-distillation framework are only described in paper B (bge-m3).

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: ModernBERT's multi-vector models are trained on 810k MS-Marco samples with teacher scores from BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024) using the PyLate library.

spans.quote:
Models are trained
on 810k samples from MS-Marco (Bajaj et al.,
2016) and teacher scores from BGE-M3 (Chen
et al., 2024), using the PyLate library (Chaffin and
Sourty, 2024).

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The M3-Embedding (BGE-M3) paper proposes a self-knowledge-distillation framework in which the [CLS] embedding is used for dense retrieval while other token embeddings are used for sparse and multi-vector retrieval, and the relevance scores of the different retrieval functions are integrated as the teacher signal.

spans.quote:
Firstly, we propose a novelself knowl-
edge distillationframework, where the multiple
retrieval functionalities can be jointly learned and
mutually reinforced. In M3-Embedding, the [CLS]
embedding is used for dense retrieval, while embed-
dings from other tokens are used for sparse retrieval
and multi-vector retrieval.

Thus, we integrate the relevance scores
from different retrieval functions as the teacher
signal, which is used to enhance the learning pro-
cess via knowledge distillation.

questions.question: ColBERTv2's related work describes a family of sparse retrieval models that produce a sparse vocabulary-level vector with one dimension per token and that it treats as a central point of comparison. In the paper that introduced the first model of that family, which two ingredients produce the highly sparse representations, and how many training stages does the approach need?
questions.expected_answer: The family is SPLADE. The SPLADE paper presents a first-stage ranker based on explicit sparsity regularization and a log-saturation effect on term weights (a logarithmic activation plus sparse regularization), which yields highly sparse representations, and states that the approach is simple and trained end-to-end in a single stage; the sparsity regularization can also be tuned to trade FLOPs against effectiveness.
questions.rationale: Paper A (colbert2) identifies the sparse family it compares against; the sparsity regularization, log-saturation and single-stage end-to-end training are only in paper B (splade). The question never names SPLADE.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: ColBERTv2's related work says SPLADE and SPLADEv2 produce a sparse vocabulary-level vector that keeps the term-level decomposition of late interaction with one dimension per token, and that SPLADEv2 is a central point of comparison in its experiments.

spans.quote:
To
produce scalar weights, SPLADE (Formal et al.,
2021b) and SPLADEv2 (Formal et al., 2021a) pro-
duce a sparse vocabulary-level vector that retains
the term-level decomposition of late interaction
while simplifying the storage into one dimension
per token.

SPLADEv2 has been shown
to be highly effective, within and across domains,
and it is a central point of comparison in the exper-
iments we report on in this paper.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The SPLADE paper presents a first-stage ranker based on explicit sparsity regularization and a log-saturation effect on term weights, trained end-to-end in a single stage, and names the model SPLADE (based on a logarithmic activation and sparse regularization).

In this work, we present
a new first-stage ranker based on explicit sparsity regularization
and a log-saturation effect on term weights, leading to highly sparse
representations and competitive results with respect to state-of-
the-art dense and sparse methods. Our approach is simple, trained

we propose the SParse Lexical AnD Ex-

Because no suitable public dataset existed, its authors created WikiEval: they first selected 50 Wikipedia pages covering events that have happened since the start of 2022, prioritising pages with recent edits, and then used ChatGPT to suggest a question answerable from each page, producing question-context-answer triples with human judgments.
questions.rationale: Paper A (ares) identifies the criticized framework; the WikiEval dataset and its 50 recent Wikipedia pages are only described in paper B (ragas). The question does not name Ragas or WikiEval.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: ARES describes the open-source RAGAS framework (James and Es, 2023) as prompting an LM to evaluate relevance of retrieved information and faithfulness and accuracy of generated responses, and criticizes such strategies for relying on a fixed set of heuristically hand-written prompts.

questions.question: In RAGChecker's meta-evaluation the strongest baseline metric is an 'Answer Similarity' metric that comes from an earlier RAG evaluation framework and is backed by text-embedding-ada-002. In that framework's own paper, how is its faithfulness score computed?
questions.expected_answer: The framework is Ragas. In the Ragas paper, faithfulness is estimated by first using an LLM to extract a set of statements S(as(q)) from the answer (decomposing long sentences into shorter assertions) and then checking each statement against the context; the final faithfulness score is F = |V| / |S|, where |V| is the number of statements supported according to the LLM and |S| is the total number of statements.
questions.rationale: Paper A (ragchecker) is the only place that names the best-performing baseline metric and its backbone; the statement-extraction procedure and the F = |V|/|S| formula are only in paper B (ragas). The question avoids naming Ragas.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: RAGChecker reports that among baseline metrics the Answer Similarity metric of RAGAS, based on the stronger backbone model text-embedding-ada-002, shows the best performance.

spans.quote:
Among other baseline metrics, Answer Similarity of RAGAS, which
is based on the stronger backbone model text-embedding-ada-002 [28], shows the best performance.

sufficient_evidence_sets.statement: The Ragas paper computes faithfulness by using an LLM to extract a set of statements from the answer and then scoring F = |V|/|S|, where |V| is the number of statements supported according to the LLM and |S| is the total number of statements.

To estimate faithfulness, we first use an LLM
to extract a set of statements, S(as(q)). The aim
of this step is to decompose longer sentences into
shorter and more focused assertions.

The final faithfulness score, F , is then computed
as F = |V|
|S| , where |V | is the number of statements
